 Learn more The Federal Reserve kicked off its two-day policy meeting on Tuesday as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers who nevertheless seem reluctant to hike rates this month. 
 Fed watchers expect the central bank to keep benchmark rates in the 3.75% to 4% range , with bond traders pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike on Wednesday, per CME Group. A rate hike in December appears far more likely, however, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures. 
 Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , several officials' remarks suggest the Fed will hold rates this month to continue assessing additional data. The proximity of the October meeting to the US midterm elections next Tuesday is also seen as a deterrent to bold monetary policy moves. 
 With the Fed holding rates steady seen as all but given, the focus is on what Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will say at his post-FOMC-meeting press conference. Warsh has deliberately avoided telegraphing future Fed policy moves, but hot inflation could elicit more insight from him into the path forward. 
 LIVE 12 updates 44 mins ago Grace O'Donnell Fed meeting began as scheduled
 A Fed spokesperson said day two of the FOMC meeting began at 9:00 a.m. ET as scheduled. 
 Traders are pricing in 90.6% odds that the Fed will hold rates steady at 2 p.m. ET today, per CME Group's FedWatch. Many are already looking ahead to the December meeting, where traders see an 84% chance of a rate hike. 
 57 mins ago Jennifer Schonberger The Fed is expected to hold rates steady. How will Warsh justify that in the face of higher inflation?
 The Federal Reserve is widely anticipated to hold interest rates steady Wednesday afternoon, less than a week before the midterm elections . A key question: How will Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh rationalize holding rates steady after the latest inflation reports have shown prices heating back up? 
 Deutsche Bank chief US economist Matt Luzzetti expects Warsh will signal that recent inflation data reinforces the need for further rate hikes over time , but that skipping October allows officials more time to assess trends. However, he noted that Warsh will need to avoid making the mistake he made at his July press conference, when he created confusion about whether the Fed was committed to a credible strategy to bring down inflation. 
 "Warsh will want to avoid any indications that the Fed is unwilling to take appropriate action against sticky inflation," Luzzetti said. 
 Read more. 
 Today at 12:00 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Former Fed vice chairman explains why it's the 'perfect time for forward guidance'
 The market is laser-focused on Kevin Warsh's press conference on Wednesday, with some economists expecting a "hawkish hold" from the Fed chair. 
 "I think this is a perfect instance to see where forward guidance would be so important," Princeton University professor of Economics and Public Affairs Alan Blinder told Yahoo Finance (see video below). 
 "Lots of people are expecting something that's called a hawkish hold," Blinder explained. "The hawkish part can only come from forward guidance, from talk. If you hold, you do nothing. You don't raise the interest rate, and that's it if you don't say anything." 
 Blinder previously served as the Fed vice chairman under President Clinton. He noted that the Fed is "stuck between the proverbial rock and a hard place" with this decision, as policymakers can make strong arguments for holding or hiking rates. 
 "But the hard place is Kevin Warsh's own doing, the way he has denigrated forward guidance," Blinder said. 
 He explained what can happen to markets when the Fed gives little indication of what it might do next. 
 "The last couple of weeks have shown you what can happen when you just leave everybody guessing," Blinder said. "The market has gyrated quite a lot in its expectations of what would happen tomorrow. I don't think the Fed has gyrated nearly that much, but the market has." 
 Today at 9:00 AM UTC Grace O'Donnell Fed officials appear divided on whether to hike now or later
 Minutes from the Fed's September meeting indicated that most FOMC members assessed that one more rate hike would be appropriate by the end of the year. 
 But officials and economists remain somewhat divided on whether a hike is needed in October or whether the Fed can wait until December to assess more data. 
 "The majority of officials still support the notion of at least some further policy firming by year end. But at the same time, there seems to be this sense of a very patient, very tepid approach to any additional rate hikes," Stifel chief economist Lindsey Piegza told Yahoo Finance. 
 Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger details the two camps: 
 The center of the Fed's interest-rate-setting committee is signaling a desire for more data and doesn't want to slow economic growth. 
 Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee told Yahoo Finance this month that hotter-than-expected September consumer inflation was "discouraging" but said he wants to wait for more data before raising interest rates further. He said core inflation remaining as high as it is now would be neither "acceptable" nor "compatible with the Fed target, and our policy needs to address that." 
 However, other Fed officials, including Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack , have said they would rather make small hikes now to rein in what they see as broadening inflation. The hawkish camp fears that waiting too long could force drastic actions later, akin to the aggressive tightening campaign the central bank was forced to mount in 2022. 
 Read more. 
 Today at 6:00 AM UTC Grace O'Donnell Should you open a CD account before the Fed's next meeting?
 Yahoo Finance's Ivana Pino writes: 
 Markets believe the Fed will hold its benchmark interest rate steady this week. However, it's not possible to predict the Fed's next move with 100% certainty. 
 If the Fed decides to raise the federal funds rate at some point this year, CD rates will soon start to increase. However, if you open a CD, you will lock in today's rates on your balance and continue earning that deposit rate. 
 If the rate hike is expected, there's a chance banks have already priced in the increase into today's CD rates. Waiting may not bring you a higher rate. 
 Even so, we can't know for sure what will happen. So, while you wait for the Fed's official announcement about how rates will change (or not), it could be a good time to evaluate where you're currently keeping your savings and consider opening a new CD . 
 Read more. 
 Today at 3:00 AM UTC Jennifer Schonberger How meeting 6 times a year instead of 8 could arm the Fed with more data
 Federal Reserve officials will walk into their policy meeting in a week and a half without a key inflation data point to inform their interest rate decision. 
 The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index will be released on Oct. 29, the day after the Fed meets. While they can use pieces of other inflation datasets to estimate this measure, one analyst points out that if the central bank met every eight weeks instead of the current six, it would have a fuller set of data available at each meeting, enabling more informed decisions. 
 "The current calendar has clear drawbacks," Deutsche Bank chief US economist Matt Luzzetti said. "The Fed could meaningfully improve the timeliness of the data available to them at FOMC meetings with relatively simple tweaks to the calendar." 
 Right now, the calendar doesn't account for when key data is released, often leaving the Fed with relatively stale data at each meeting. Not having key inflation data until a day after its meeting happens regularly. The PCE index was released within days after the April and July meetings as well. The December meeting will take place the day before the November Consumer Price Index report is released. 
 Read more. 
 Today at 12:00 AM UTC Ben Werschkul The Fed faces a politically fraught rate decision on the eve of an election for the third time in a row
 Federal Reserve interest rate changes on the eve of elections are tricky propositions, but for the third election in a row, the central bank may be unable to dodge that prospect after a hot inflation reading on Wednesday. 
 New Consumer Price Index data showed inflation heated up again in September , rising 3.7% annually and posting a 0.6% month-over-month surge. Core inflation, the measure more closely watched by the Fed, was also hotter than expected, rising 2.6% annually and 0.3% monthly. Following Wednesday's CPI release, odds of an October rate hike immediately spiked. 
 That new data comes as the next Federal Open Market Committee interest rate decision is scheduled for Oct. 28, just six days before Election Day. 
 "There is a political implication for going in October," Wolfe Research chief economist Stephanie Roth told Yahoo Finance on Wednesday, adding that committee members "would very much prefer not to do it," but the data is making a rate hike a distinct possibility. 
 "This makes the October meeting live," Roth said of the inflation reading. 
 Read more. 
 Tue, October 27, 2026 at 9:25 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Federal Reserve part of busy week for central bank decisions
 Markets are heading into a busy few days for global central bank rate announcements. 
 Five major central banks are scheduled to make policy decisions this week, with two expected to hike and three to hold. 
 On Wednesday, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Bank of Canada will announce their decisions before the Fed releases its FOMC statement. Both central banks are expected to hike rates. 
 In Canada's case, the BOC is caught between a weakening economy and higher inflation. Governor Tiff Macklem has signaled in recent months that he is concerned about higher oil prices bleeding through to broader price inflation. 
 The next day, the European Central Bank is expected to hold rates steady, as is the Bank of Japan on Friday. 
 Many economists see the overall bias of central banks tilting toward tighter policy next year as artificial intelligence and the war in the Middle East drive inflation higher. 
 "If you're a central banker ... you've got to recognize this as a shock," Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said about AI at the IMF annual meeting this month. 
 Tue, October 27, 2026 at 8:19 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Stocks close higher ahead of Fed decision day
 The major US stock indexes rose on Tuesday as investors anticipated the Fed's decision on Wednesday. 
 The Dow ( ^DJI ) edged just above the flat line, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) rose 0.6% and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) gained 1.2% amid a semiconductor stock rally. 
 The US dollar index ( DX-Y.NYB ) rose above 102, and the 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) remained steady at 4.99%. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) also rose to above $80,600. 
 Conviction that the Fed would hold rates steady firmed on Tuesday, with traders expecting just 7% odds of a hike. Unless the Fed opts for a surprise hike, the decision is unlikely to move markets much. 
 But watch what happens to assets when Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh begins speaking tomorrow. Investors will be on alert for any hawkish signals. 
 Tue, October 27, 2026 at 5:54 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell What time is the Fed meeting?
 The Federal Open Market Committee's two-day policy meeting has started and will conclude at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday. 
 The FOMC's decision on whether to cut, hold, or raise interest rates will be released at 2 p.m. tomorrow. Following that decision, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will hold a news conference at 2:30 p.m. that will be live-streamed. 
 This is the seventh FOMC meeting this year. The final Fed meeting of the year will take place from Dec. 8-9 and will include a Summary of Economic Projections, which will be used to gauge where policymakers see rates heading in 2027. 
 Read more. 
 Tue, October 27, 2026 at 3:25 PM UTC Jennifer Schonberger Fed expected to hold rates steady this week despite hot inflation — but signal they're not done hiking
 The Federal Reserve heads into its interest-rate decision this week facing hotter inflation, keeping the meeting live even as markets widely expect the central bank to hold interest rates steady just days before the midterm elections. 
 Alan Blinder, a former Fed vice chair and a Princeton University economics professor, is expecting a "hawkish pause." 
 Although Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh doesn't favor telegraphing the central bank's next move, Blinder said the moment calls for clarity. 
 "This is a perfect time for clear forward guidance that doesn't quite say, but strongly hints, we're pausing now, but we stand ready to raise again and even give a hint that the next meeting might be the next interest rate hike." 
 Read more.

 Tue, October 27, 2026 at 3:03 PM UTC Grace O'Donnell Fed meeting kicks off as traders broadly expect no hike
 The Federal Reserve's two-day policy meeting kicked off this morning at 9:30 a.m. ET, as scheduled, a Fed spokesperson confirmed. 
 Expectations remain firm that the Fed will hold rates steady in a range of 3.75% to 4% after hiking by 25 basis points in September. Traders broadly view that the Fed will hike again in December. 
 But in October, there's a strong belief the Fed won't move rates. According to CME Group's FedWatch, traders see a 90% chance of no move.
